entries.title: In Germany record heat meets climate action fatigue
entries.summary: For the German government climate action does not seem to be a priority — despite record temperatures, heat-related deaths and drought. Why don't more people take to the streets in protest?
entries.content:
Germany

In Germany record heat meets climate action fatigue

August 14, 2026

For the German government climate action does not seem to be a priority — despite record temperatures, heat-related deaths and drought. Why don't more people take to the streets in protest?

When Lars Werner of the "Last Generation" glued himself to the road four years ago to protest for greater climate action, Germany had not yet seen 12,500 heat-related deaths (Germany's number for 2026 so far), or record temperatures across western Europe, and fully loaded ships were still navigating the Rhine without difficulty.

"Of course, I could say 'I told you so,' because it was foreseeable and comes as no surprise whatsoever," Werner tells DW.

"The fact is, even back then, I was constantly explaining in my presentations that the Rhine would eventually run dry during hot summers and that this would have an incredible impact on the economy."

Something very strange is happening in Germany in the summer of 2026: While entire villages are being evacuated due to forest fires, farmers are losing around their harvest to drought, and hospital patients and the elderly in nursing homes face an acute threat to their lives in buildings with no air conditioning, the federal government remains astonishingly quiet.

Despite the crisis, it has still not convened a "heat summit."

"It is utterly irrational for the federal government to resort to tinkering with regulations — such as lifting the Sunday ban on truck traffic — in the hope of somehow scraping by without implementing a comprehensive climate protection policy for the long or even short term," Werner argues.

Fridays for Future Germany: not the same group from a few years ago

The government no longer has to worry about "Last Generation" protesters calling out its inaction by setting up road blockades. The climate activists halted their protests two years ago, worn down by hostility, fines and prison sentences. Now, the task of fiercely criticizing political decision-makers on climate policy falls primarily to the Fridays for Future Germany (FFF) movement.

"The federal government is doing virtually nothing when it comes to effective climate policy. Instead, various 'pseudo-solutions' are being promoted — such as dredging the Rhine to make it deeper or lifting the Sunday driving ban for trucks," FFF spokesperson Linda Kastrup told DW. She deplores what she sees as short-term fixes for the symptoms of the climate crisis, and notes that effectively nothing sustainable is being done.

Only a few hundred protesters turned out for a demonstration outside the Chancellery in Berlin a week ago. It was a far cry from the protests in 2019, prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, when hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets to demand climate action.

A recent study by the Bertelsmann Foundation found that 80% of people in Germany are worried about climate change, and more than 50% want to see more government spending on climate protection. But that doesn't mean they take to the streets.

Kastrup is not surprised.

"When Chancellor Friedrich Merz completely dismisses and ignores climate policy — when we see tens of thousands of heat-related deaths in Germany alone yet not a single word is said about it — it inevitably leaves people with the impression in their private lives that climate protection doesn't matter. Naturally, that makes it very difficult to motivate people to take to the streets," she says.

In addition, there has been a rise in hateful speech directed at climate activists on social media.

"Two days ago, I posted a reel and within a very short time, there were 2,000 hateful comments on it," says Kastrup.

Focus shifted to Ukraine, Gaza

Sebastian Haunss, a researcher in political science at the University of Bremen, says it is surprising that the scorching summer of 2026 has not led to climate protests. He finds it remarkable that on the one hand, more and more people in Germany are installing solar power systems, but on the other, they take vacations on environmentally damaging cruise ships.

He sees several reasons for this development.

"A strong counter-position has emerged," he says. "Specifically, political actors like the AfD [the far-right populist Alternative for Germany Party, Eds.] are pursuing an agenda that opposes climate protection regulations. Such actors — whether at the international or national level — did not exist just a few years ago."

Also, Haunss points out that large organizations like Fridays for Future have been replaced by a vast number of local groups, who operate largely out of the public eye. However, a pivotal event could bring people back onto the streets in large numbers at any moment, he says.

"Then there is the competition for attention; the COVID pandemic and the war in Ukraine pushed the climate issue out of the spotlight, and current economic concerns also play a major role," says Haunss, adding that many of those who took to the streets against climate change a few years ago are now focusing on different topics: "In some cases, their issues have shifted, and other topics — such as the war in Gaza and solidarity with Palestine — have moved to the forefront:"

A divided government

German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) now wants to amend the constitution, the Basic Law, to make heat protection a joint responsibility of the federal government, the states, and the municipalities. However, the larger coalition partner, the center-right bloc of the Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU), is skeptical and cites "legal concerns."

"Within the coalition, I do indeed see us — the SPD — as the bulwark for energy transition to renewables," Nina Scheer, energy policy spokesperson for the SPD parliamentary group, tells DW. "All my colleagues in our parliamentary group would like to achieve more in terms of climate protection. But we also have to accept setbacks regarding climate measures in order to maintain unity within the coalition."

For instance, she says, she voted in favor of making air travel cheaper and expanding regional airports, although she personally finds it wrong.

Scheer has long advocated for a faster expansion of renewable energy, and does not see eye to eye with Economics Minister Katherina Reiche (CDU), who favors gas over wind and solar power for energy supply.

"Reiche goes around pushing the narrative that while we do want climate protection and remain committed to the goals, renewables are simply too expensive. And to that, one has to say: 'No, that is simply not true,'" says Scheer.

Under the Paris Agreement and the national Climate Action Act, Germany has committed to achieving climate neutrality by 2045. However, recent statements by some politicians raise doubts as to whether the federal government is pursuing this goal with great determination.

"We cannot halt climate change from Germany alone," said Chancellor Friedrich Merz recently.

SPD politician Scheer considers this a disastrous statement.

"Fundamentally, it is a rejection of greater climate action, even though we ought to be stepping up our efforts," she says.

This article has been translated from German.

entries.title: Luigi Mangione pleads guilty to federal stalking charges in Brian Thompson death
entries.summary: The plea resolves the remaining federal charges tied to the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson and could affect a separate New York state case.
entries.content:
August 14, 2026

The plea resolves the remaining federal charges tied to the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson and could affect a separate New York state case.

Luigi Mangione pleaded guilty in a Manhattan federal court to stalking charges tied to the death of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson.

"I shot Mr. Thompson in Manhattan and he died," he told the court.

Prosecutors said Mangione traveled to New York City and fatally shot Thompson outside a Manhattan hotel on December 4, 2024, as he walked to UnitedHealth Group's annual investor conference.

The judge has accepted his guilty plea and said sentencing would take place in December. Mangione faces a possible sentence ‌of life without parole on the two counts of stalking.

Mangione's lawyer seeks dismissal of state murder charges

Mangione had previously pleaded not guilty to federal murder, weapons and stalking charges. Earlier this year, the judge dismissed the murder and weapons counts on legal technicalities, leaving only the stalking charges and eliminating the possibility of the death penalty.

Mangione still seperately faces murder, weapons and forgery charges in New York state court. 

Outside federal court, Mangione's lawyer, Karen Friedman Agnifilo, told reporters that "state charges must be dismissed under New York's double jeopardy protections."

Under double jeopardy protections, defendants are protected from being prosecuted for the same crime twice.

How Mangione explained his guilty plea to the court

Mangione told the federal court he pursued Thompson "after years of enduring severe pain from a broken back and navigating the obstacles of the health insurance system."

Thompson was chief executive of UnitedHealthcare, one of the largest health insurers in the United States.

He was walking into a Midtown Manhattan hotel for the annual investor day when he was shot three times in the back.

Mangione said he then used a 3D printer to make part of the gun used in the shooting.

The killing underscored widespread frustration with the US healthcare system, and some supporters portrayed Mangione as a hero.

Conservatives, including President Donald Trump, however, have called for a tough punishment.

Jamie McDonald, the Manhattan US attorney, told reporters that his office would seek a sentence of life imprisonment.

"There can be no celebrity in assassination," he said.

Outside the courthouse, a man shouted "America loves Luigi" at relatives of Thompson as they left court Friday in a convoy of black SUVs.

Thompson's family said in a statement that the plea marked an "important step toward justice."

"We look to the court to ensure that sentencing reflects the severity of this crime," the family said.

Edited by: Rob Turner

entries.title: Germany news: Car industry hemorrhaging jobs
entries.summary: The country's famed auto sector is losing jobs faster than any industrial branch in the economy, official statistics show. Meanwhile, farmers say drought conditions could affect this year's harvest. DW has more.
entries.content:
Published August 14, 2026last updated August 14, 2026

The country's famed auto sector is losing jobs faster than any industrial branch in the economy, official statistics show. Meanwhile, farmers say drought conditions could affect this year's harvest. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Friday, August 14, 2026:

  • A wildfire near the Belgian border has forced around 1,800 people to leave their homes
  • Amid high temperatures, farmers say drought could badly damage grain, potato, vegetable and feed crop harvests
  • Germany's car sector is losing jobs faster than any industrial sector in the economy

For coverage of the wildfire in western Germany click on our dedicated blog here

Don't let the algorithm hide the news. If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google so you'll always see our verified news first.

Skip next section Extreme athlete arrives in Cologne after swimming from Frankfurt

Extreme athlete arrives in Cologne after swimming from Frankfurt

Nathalie Pohl has completed her four-day swin down the Main and Rhine rivers from Frankfurt to Cologne.

The 31-year-old extreme swimmer started the aquatic journey of more than 200 kilometers (124 miles) on Tuesday morning, arriving on the banks of the Rhine in Cologne on Friday afternoon.

Her aim was to raise awareness on the importance of safe swimming among children, and to fund swimming projects. Her team says they managed to raise around €616,000 ($713,000) in total.

"Every child has the right to feel secure in the water," she said upon arrival. At the same time she was keen to point out that her challenge shouldn't be taken as a "false signal."

"Especially in the Rhine, far too many people still drown," she said. "It's not bathing water."

Skip next section Germany sees rise in new business registrations

Germany sees rise in new business registrations

Germany saw a noticeable rise in new business registrations in the first half of this year. Around 352,400 new businesses were registered, up 8.3% compared with the same period last year, according to the Federal Statistical Office.

Of these, around 69,600 were considered businesses of greater economic significance — for example because of their legal form or because they planned to employ staff. That was 3.0% more than a year earlier.

At the same time, the number of complete business closures in this category fell by 3.8% to around 49,800.

Skip next section Farmers fear drought will wipe out this year's harvest

Farmers fear drought will wipe out this year's harvest

German farmers fear they could see harvests wiped out entirely by ongoing drought and unseasonably high temperatures, says German Farmers' Association (DBV) President Joachim Ruckwied.

"We expect below-average grain harvests, especially when it comes to wheat and rapeseed," he said during an interview with Germany's Redaktionsnetzwerk media group.

"As far as fall crops are concerned, the trend suggests we must expect significant yield losses here as well."

Potatoes, vegetables and sugar beets, as well as grain maize and soy could be affected.

Ruckwied warned that although farmers in the north could hope for "acceptable" if "below-average" harvests thanks to occasional rains, farmers in drier southern Germany could be facing "total harvest loss."

"What's becoming a problem, especially in southern Germany, is that feed crops aren't coming in," he added, noting that this would force farmers to slaughter animals earlier than usual.

The threat adds to the financial pressure farmers already face when it comes to buying seed, fertilizer and pesticides, says Ruckwied.

"The economic situation is brutal… on the one hand high investment costs, and on the other, lower market prices for agricultural products."

Skip next section Dramatic rescue in Berlin high-rise fire

Dramatic rescue in Berlin high-rise fire

Several people were injured Friday morning when fire broke out in a 21-story apartment complex in Berlin's Friedrichshain neighborhood, near the Ostbahnhof train station.

The blaze started on the 11th floor, say firefighters, and quickly spread to floors above.

A fire department spokesperson described the situation as "dramatic."

Witnesses say numerous residents stood at windows and balconies prepared to jump rather than be consumed by smoke and flames.

Although jump cushions were installed as a precaution below, these were not used and authorities say residents were retrieved from a stairwell with a rescue ladder.

Some 130 fire, police and emergency services personnel were in action before residents could be saved and the fire extinguished.

Smoke damage is said to have been extensive, causing at least five injuries, and leaving roughly 70 people to be cared for on site.

The cause of the fire is unclear, though police are treating it as a possible balcony fire.

Skip next section German hiker injured in Alps fall

German hiker injured in Alps fall

A 66-year old German hiker was seriously injured in a fall in the Austrian Alps on Friday according to authorities in Nesselwängle, Tyrol.

Emergency services say the man slipped and fell a few meters, losing consciousness before falling over a second, 40-meter-high (132-foot) cliff.

The man's daughter and others administered first-aid and contacted mountain rescue. He was airlifted to an Innsbruck hospital.

On Thursday, a 36-year-old German died in a fall in Zillertal, Tyrol. A few days earlier, a 74-year-old German similarly died from a fall in East Tyrol.

Skip next section Almost half of Bundestag sign up to new 'opt-out' organ donor model

Almost half of Bundestag sign up to new 'opt-out' organ donor model

More than 200 lawmakers in the lower house of parliament, the Bundestag, have signed up to a cross-party initiative seeking to change Germany's organ donor rules.

The proposal seeks to move from an "opt-in" system to an "opt-out" one. 

At present, people in Germany have to carry a donor card, register as an organ donor, or otherwise inform healthcare professionals of their willingness to donate in a legally binding manner before death. If they do not, and they are deemed potentially viable donors, sometimes their next of kin are asked to decide on their behalf — a traumatic and difficult decision in the midst of a bereavement.

With donor rates consistently failing to meet demand, some medical professionals have long advocated a system where instead of declaring your willingness to donate, you are assumed to be a potential donor unless you specifically say you are not a willing participant.

A draft law has been put forward in the Bundestag — not as a government initiative but as a cross party conscience vote, typically for causes with only a narrow chance of success but which politicians nevertheless wish to put in the spotlight.

In this case, however, 245 lawmakers have already signed the motion, in a chamber with 630 politicians. If the bill could gather some more support during the parliamentary process, it might have a chance of progressing.

Parliamentary debate on the bill is scheduled after lawmakers return from the summer break.

Around 8,000 people are currently on donor waiting lists in Germany.

Skip next section Catamaran passenger ferry crashes into Lake Constance harbor wall

Catamaran passenger ferry crashes into Lake Constance harbor wall

A catamaran passenger ferry has crashed on Lake Constance, colliding with the harbor wall.

Police said that 12 people were injured, and it was not immediately clear how seriously. They were receiving treatment on site.

Images showed that the ship had collided head-on with the harbor wall, sustaining quite considerable damage. It was still afloat, however.

Police said there was no fuel leak and no environmental hazard posed by the incident. What caused the early morning carsh was not immediately clear.

The hourly catamaran ferry brings people across Lake Constance, or the Bodensee in German, from Konstanz to Friedrichshafen.

Skip next section Car industry hemorrhaging jobs

Car industry hemorrhaging jobs

Germany's automotive branch is losing jobs faster than any industrial sector in the economy according to the Federal Statistical Office Destatis.

The car industry is second only to mechanical engineering when it comes to size, yet its employment numbers are now at their lowest since 2005.

At the end of the first half of 2026, 691,500 people were employed in Germany's leading industry, a drop of 42,300 workers, or 5.8%, within a single year.

Destatis said manufacturing employment fell by 2.7% overall but had fallen by 7.6% in the automobile sector. Smaller segments within the car sector fell by 10%, whereas manufacturers themselves registered a 6.1% drop in employment.

In May, Germany's Association of the Automobile Industry (VDA) warned that the sector stands to lose as many as 225,000 jobs by 2035.

Numerous German manufacturers, such as VW, Audi and Porsche, have all cut jobs in an effort to remain lean in the face of rising Chinese competition and punitive US tariffs.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Tag from the DW newsroom in Bonn.

The major talking point on another hot, dry day in Germany is the wildfire near the Dutch and Belgian border. We've got a dedicated blog running on that story, but over here is a wrap of the other topics of the day.

Including more damaging news for the once mighty car industry, and a sharp warning from farmers on the outcome of this years crop yield.

Read on for more.

entries.title: France: Top watchdog blocks social media ban for children
entries.summary: Denying access to platforms such as Facebook, TikTok and YouTube for under-15s would infringe upon freedom of expression, the Constitutional Council has said.
entries.content:
August 14, 2026

Denying access to platforms such as Facebook, TikTok and YouTube for under-15s would infringe upon freedom of expression, the Constitutional Council has said.

France's highest constitutional authority on Friday struck down the ban on social media for children under 15.

The Constitutional Council ruled that the flagship policy of President Emmanuel Macron's second term infringed on freedom of expression.

"By prohibiting minors under the age of 15 from accessing certain online services, the law inherently requires every person, even an adult, to prove their age before accessing them," it said in its decision.

The Council is a review body that ensures laws comply with the Constitution.

Macron still wants social media ban for children

French lawmakers last month approved legislation that barred children under 15 from opening social media accounts from September 1. Beyond that, platforms would have until the start of 2027 to close children's existing accounts.

The law would also have banned the use of mobile phones in high schools and required social media platforms to introduce age-verification measures in accordance with France's privacy regulator.

The Council, however, found lawmakers had failed to set out clear rules on how people should prove their age and what limits should apply, meaning there were not enough legal safeguards in place.

Macron has instructed Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu to revise the bill to address the Constitutional Council's concerns, the Elysee Palace said. It added the president wanted the reform in place before France's 2027 presidential election.

Social media bans for teens and children also considered elsewhere

Australia became the first country in the world to ban social media for under-16s in 2025. France was the first in Europe.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen last month pledged to pursue an EU-wide social media ban for children following a recommendation by an expert group to restrict access for under-13s.

"Our children need time in the real world. Time to play, time to build friendships, time to make mistakes. Time to shape their own identity, their own personality, before an algorithm shapes them instead," von der Leyen told reporters in Brussels.

"This is not about whether children can access social media. It is about whether and when social media can access our children," she said.

A number of other countries have announced plans to consider similar bans, including Brazil, the UK, Canada, Norway and Denmark.

Edited by: Rob Turner

entries.title: Eco wins: A Dutch gym for crops, a climate-ready city and a beaver comeback
entries.summary: Dutch crops hit the "climate gym," a German city is constructing for more extreme weather, and beavers are restoring rivers across Europe. This week's eco wins are all about building for a changing climate.
entries.content:
August 14, 2026

Dutch crops hit the "climate gym," a German city is preparing for more extreme weather, and beavers are restoring rivers across Europe. This week's eco wins are all about building and adapting to a changing climate.

The Netherlands: putting plants through their paces

How will the world feed 10 billion people with less land, less water, and more unpredictable weather? The Netherlands, also known as the "Silicon Valley" of agriculture and seeds, knows a thing or two about it. 

It's already the world's second largest exporter of agricultural products after the United States, despite being a fraction of the size.

Now, in some of the country's greenhouses, scientists are using high-tech means, as well as reams of data, to figure out which crops will be most resilient in a changing climate.

A German city is re-inventing itself amid a new climate reality

In October 2023, the northern German city of Kiel saw the worst storm surge in more than 150 years. It destroyed dikes, collapsed coastal cliffs and devastated marinas. It shocked city officials into reimagining infrastructure to cope with more frequent and intense weather extremes linked to human-made climate change. 

Ideas range from cool city corridors and green facades to flooding soccer pitches at certain times of the year and adapting daily schedules to heat. Find out more about what Kiel is doing, alongside other cities worldwide.

Turtles are getting ready for their close-up

Ever dreamed of becoming a wildlife photographer? Destinations in Egypt are getting tourists to snap photos of sea turtles to help with conservation efforts.

These underwater creatures have unique markings on their faces — almost like human fingerprints. Researchers use them to identify individual turtles and even track injuries. If they spot a turtle that's recovering, they can alert authorities to steer boat traffic away from that area.

Beavers make a comeback to help fight wildfires, droughts and floods

After being hunted to near extinction for their fur, meat and scent glands in the early 20th century in Europe, beavers are so back.

Thanks to major long-term rewilding efforts across the continent, populations have skyrocketed from about 1,500 wild Eurasian beavers in 1900 to 1.5 million today.

Beavers are the engineers of the animal world. They build dams that help filter water pollutants, reduce the impacts of flooding, wildfire and drought, and recharge underground aquifers. And they're fixing wetlands and rivers across Europe — from Spain to Russia.

Edited by: Louise Osborne

entries.title: Taliban pressured by insurgents after 5 years in power
entries.summary: The Taliban managed to retake power in Afghanistan on August 15, 2021. Now, they face armed factions who challenge the Taliban rule and strain their central claim of providing security.
entries.content:
Afghanistan

Taliban pressured by insurgents after 5 years in power

August 14, 2026

The Taliban managed to retake power in Afghanistan on August 15, 2021. Now, they face armed factions who challenge the Taliban rule and strain their central claim of providing security.

Less than a month before the five-year anniversary of the Taliban retaking power in Afghanistan, the Islamist regime lost control of the Yaftal-e Payeen district capital in the northeastern province of Badakhshan. The disruption was temporary, but it nevertheless marked the first time the Taliban lost control of a district center since returning to power in August 2021.

Reports from Badakhshan also indicated internal clashes among Taliban fighters and fatal attacks on high-ranking Taliban officials.

On August 2, some two weeks after the brief loss of the district center, former Afghan army general Sami Sadat ordered his forces to launch attacks against the Taliban across the country.

"Today at 5:00 AM, I ordered all military members of the United Front to begin military operations," General Sadat said in a video message released from the US, where he has lived since the fall of Afghanistan to the Taliban.

Other armed groups, including the National Resistance Front led by the son of the late commander Ahmad Shah Massoud, have been engaged in a continuous armed struggle against the Taliban since 2021. While armed insurgents have not been able to pose a major threat to the Taliban's overall grip on power, experts are questioning whether the clashes in Badakhshan could pave the way for more impactful resistance.

"In these five years, this opposition existed in two forms: political and military... As the five-year mark approaches, both forms of opposition have taken shape," former Afghan Interior Minister Mohammad Umer Daudzai told DW.

Fear of new proxy wars in Afghanistan

The Taliban have reigned with an iron fist since the collapse of the US-backed Afghan government five years ago. The Islamist regime denied basic human rights and imposed strict restrictions on women, banning them from work and education beyond the sixth grade. Women are mostly banned from public life in Afghanistan as well, and have few rights at all.

Most former government officials are in exile. While the Taliban maintain that all Afghans are free to return and lead ordinary lives, opponents counter that return is only viable if political activity is permitted.

While the regime managed to cultivate some contacts internationally, they are still viewed as illegitimate by most of the world's governments. To date, only Russia has acknowledged the Taliban as the official government of Afghanistan.

Facing pressures both within and outside of the country, the Taliban repeatedly pointed to the restoration of nationwide security as their primary claim to legitimacy. However, experts warn that their governing style could in fact enable armed rebels to challenge them in various parts of Afghanistan.

"If this policy of the Taliban continues, armed forces will emerge against them, opposition will emerge, interference from neighbors will arise, and ultimately the ground will be prepared for proxy wars," former Acting Minister of Defense Shahmohammad Miakhel told DW.

Beyond political opposition, the regional branch of the "Islamic State" (IS) remains active in Afghanistan. The group has claimed responsibility for several high-profile attacks against Taliban officials, including a January explosion at a Chinese restaurant in central Kabul that killed at least seven people, and a December 2024 suicide bombing in Kabul that killed the regime's Minister of Refugees Khalil Ur-Rahman Haqqani.

Taliban claim Pakistan supports insurgents in Afghanistan

The strongest challenge to Taliban control could originate from outside Afghanistan's borders. Relations between Afghanistan and Pakistan — once considered one of the Taliban's closest allies — have been fraught with tension since 2021, erupting in full on clashes this year. According to a United Nations report from May, cross-border hostilities during the first three months of 2026 resulted in at least 372 Afghan civilian deaths and nearly 400 injuries.

"When Mr. Sami Sadat issues such an order from America to those who must fight the Taliban, he has certainly seen a green light. And remember that in Afghanistan, no group and no one can carry out any activity without the support of one or more foreign countries," former defense ministry spokesperson Mohammad Radmanish told DW.

While the Taliban publicly downplay the threat posed by rebel groups, they also allege that external support for armed resistance is rising.

"We are aware that lame ducks were invited to Pakistan [...] A large group has been invited to Islamabad who are now discussing where they can have an office and center and refuge," Taliban spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid told DW in an interview.

When pressed by DW to provide evidence for these claims, Mujahid offered no proof.

'Islamabad has used all its options'

Pakistan accuses the Taliban of providing safe havens to militants executing attacks inside Pakistani territory, particularly the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP). The Taliban deny these charges, in turn accusing Pakistan of harboring hostile elements and violating Afghan sovereignty.

Qamar Cheema, an Islamabad-based security expert, told DW in February that it is Pakistan that is targeting the militant groups.

"Pakistan wants the Afghan people to understand that the Taliban are harboring terrorists. Therefore, Pakistan will continue targeting military sites associated with the Taliban, TTP and ISIS-K hideouts," Cheema said.

"Islamabad has used all its options, including regional diplomacy and direct communication, but nothing has been honored," he added. "As a neighboring Muslim country, Pakistan appears to inflict damage in an attempt to alter Taliban behavior."

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

entries.title: Congo: Ebola cases are rising at record pace
entries.summary: The Ebola virus is spreading rapidly in the DRC. In Kinshasa, a city of millions, fears of a serious health crisis are growing. Hospitals are scrambling to prepare for emergencies as best as they can.
entries.content:
Democratic Republic of Congo

Congo: Ebola cases rising at record pace

August 14, 2026

The Ebola virus is spreading rapidly in the DRC. In Kinshasa, a city of millions, fears of a serious health crisis are growing. Hospitals are scrambling to prepare for emergencies as best as they can.

The Ebola epidemic in the eastern part of the Democratic Republic of the Congo has now spread to a sixth province in the country. Concerns are growing that the life-threatening infectious disease could reach the capital, Kinshasa, which is home to 19 million people.

Facilities for isolating patients are ready for the event that a public health alert should hit the capital, says Jean-Jacques Muyembe, Director General of the National Institute for Biomedical Research (INRB).

"If there is a suspected case, the epidemiological services and the INRB laboratory are ready to quickly identify and confirm cases," he told DW.

"The Ministry of Health has set up the Cinquantenaire Hospital so that it can admit and fully isolate patients if necessary. We are prepared. We can quickly contain an Ebola outbreak here in Kinshasa."

A health crisis still in the making

However, the virus has been spreading faster than health authorities can contain it. This Ebola outbreak is driven by the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus, for which no vaccine or treatment has yet been approved.

According to Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization (WHO), the outbreak, given its rapid rise, could surpass the West African Ebola outbreak of 2014 – 2016. .

At that time, 11,000 people died, while the current health crisis has claimed 2,000 lives so far, with more than 4,300 cases recorded to date. Authorities officially announced the outbreak on May 15; three months later, the country remains on edge.

The WHO meanwhile expects the current outbreak to only peak in six months.

The initial infections meanwhile can be traced back to as early as February, according to reports. The epicenter of the outbreak was identified as the northeastern province of Ituri, which has been plagued by insecurity for years, and is home to a large number of internally displaced persons.

Many other cases have meanwhile also been reported in the provinces of North and South Kivu, where the security situation is an even bigger problem; authorities have effectively lost control over entire areas in their years-long conflict with M23 rebels and affiliated groups.

Fear among Kinshasa's massive population

Fear among the population of contracting the virus is also growing every day. A week ago, the threat came close to the capital when a boat was stopped at the port of Maluku, about 65 kilometers upstream from Kinshasa.

One of the passengers had previously disembarked in Mongala Province to seek medical help, presenting with typical Ebola symptoms such as fever and diarrhea.

Shortly thereafter, the patient died, prompting more than 200 passengers from the vessel to be placed in isolation. Teams from the Ministry of Health and the WHO tested them using a mobile laboratory — but the results came back negative.

But with its population of millions, this did not mean the all-clear for Kinshasa: Every day people come and go between cities and provinces, leaving potentially lethal traces behind.

In fact, the rapid spread of the current outbreak has been positively attributed to large-scale population movements as well as ongoing violence in main affected areas.

Not enough beds for worst-case scenario

Beyond the diagnosis of the disease and isolation of patients, capacity remains one of the biggest challenges for Kinshasa if the virus were to make its way there.

However, the Center for Public Health Emergency Response (COUSP) says that it plans to further expand its capacity to be able to meet the onset of any outbreak.

Emergency preparations have already been taken at Cinquantenaire Hospital: "We have set up twenty beds for this purpose. However, this capacity is flexible and can be expanded to 200 or 250 beds," Christian Ngandu, the hospital's coordinator, told DW. 

However, according to the WHO, several thousand beds would need to be ready in the worst-case scenario.

"We are currently exploring the possibility of providing additional beds. We have trained more than 120 people from various facilities, including the Vijana, Sino-Congolais, Kinkole, Kintambo and Cinquantenaire hospitals. These professionals are capable of treating any potential Ebola case," Ngandu said.

Is enough being done?

According to Carlos Mupili, president of the Supreme Council of Civil Society, current capacities are insufficient.

"Twenty beds are insignificant in this city, and a single hospital is not enough. Several health facilities should have been mobilized to prevent the outbreak effectively," he told DW.

Mupili has been calling on authorities to provide more resources to avoid unpleasant surprises: "The authorities must act swiftly and provide the necessary resources so we are not overwhelmed and... forced to make hasty decisions."

WHO Director-General Ghebreyesus cautioned that an unexpected surge in infections could ensue anywhere, as contact-tracing of infected individuals has been slow. He expressed "concern" about the fact that many people dying from the virus have not been registered on the official Ebola contact lists before being buried.

Furthermore, he stressed that many infections originate from from funerals.

Ngandu meanwhile emphasizes the fact that there has not been a single case of Ebola in Kinshasa so far, and that the primary strategy is to keep things that way.

To break the fast-moving chains of transmission, 95% of all contacts must be tracked; currently, that rate is believe to be around only 80%.

Scientists meanwhile are scrambling to find a cure: Clinical trials of two anti-viral treatments are underway, and work on vaccines is also in progress. The results — so far — look promising.

To date, there have been no mutations of the virus observed in the current DRC outbreak, commented Sylvie Briand, the WHO's chief scientist, which has been a small source of hope amid the growing crisis. After all, mutations of the virus could be highly dangerous, with the potential of becoming more lethal or increasing the transmission rate, thus jumping across borders faster.

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

entries.title: Fact check: False claims target US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed
entries.summary: Abdul El-Sayed, who could become the first Muslim elected to the US Senate if he wins in November, has been targeted by false claims online following his victory in Michigan's Democratic Senate primary.
entries.content:
United States of America

Fact check: False claims target El-Sayed after primary win

August 14, 2026

Abdul El-Sayed, who could become the first Muslim elected to the US Senate if he wins in November, has been targeted by false claims online following his victory in Michigan's Democratic Senate primary.

On August 4, Abdul El-Sayed, a leading progressive candidate, won Michigan's Democratic primary for the US Senate. 

The 41-year-old will face Republican Mike Rogers in the November 3 midterm elections. The winner will succeed retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters.

Michigan is a battleground or so-called "swing" state, where both parties have a strong chance of winning. The large Arab American and Muslim population plays a key role.

If El-Sayed wins in November, he would become the first Muslim US senator in history.

Soon after his primary victory, several false claims about El-Sayed were spread online, including claims promoted by prominent political figures.

According to Lawrence Pintak, a journalism professor at Washington State University and author of America & Islam, El-Sayed is an ideal target for political disinformation.

"He checks off all the boxes: He's a Muslim, he's a progressive, and he is vocally critical of Israel," Pintak said in a written statement to DW.

DW Fact check examined claims about voting irregularities during the primaries, El-Sayed's political ideology and whether he said the US deserved the 9/11 attacks.

Alleged ghost votes

Claim: "Of course they cheated. Nobody actually votes for communists," a Facebook post claimed, linking to an article headlined: "Abdul El-Sayed got three times as many votes in Detroit as there are registered voters."

The article states that El-Sayed "received 1.4 million votes in Detroit alone — a city with approximately 480,000 registered voters."

DW Fact check: False

The Facebook account that shared the claim, "America's Last Line of Defense," states that "nothing on this page is real." The page has around 748,000 followers and is linked to a website run by Christopher Blair, a well-known creator of fabricated political content. The BBC once described him as the "godfather of fake news."

However, this disclaimer is often lost when the content is reposted on other pages, allowing the false claim to spread without context.

The invented story echoes a claim shared by US President Donald Trump days earlier about a county in Michigan: "Miracles happen in Wayne County, including more votes being cast than there are voters, by a lot." 

Trump did not provide any evidence to support his claim of alleged voter fraud.

According to the Michigan Voter Information Center, Michigan has approximately 7.3 million active registered voters, while El-Sayed received 743,455 votes statewide in the Democratic Senate primary, not 1.4 million votes in Detroit alone.

Michael Hameleers, an associate professor of political communication at the University of Amsterdam who researches misinformation and disinformation, warned about the impact of such allegations.

"It is a prominent delegitimization technique to put democratic institutions and the fairness of elections in question," he said.

"Especially in a context where people perceive disinformation and fraud as highly likely, it may be a fruitful strategy to cast doubt on elections."

A 2023 US study found that exposure to unfounded claims of voter fraud can significantly undermine confidence in elections, particularly among Republicans and Trump supporters.

Claims about political ideology

Claim: US President Donald Trump has repeatedly described Abdul El-Sayed as a communist, most recently in a Truth Social post published shortly after El-Sayed's primary victory.

DW Fact check: False

El-Sayed's campaign has focused on government-sponsored health insurance, taxing billionaires and reducing the influence of corporate money in politics.

In the past, he has rejected claims that he is a socialist or a communist by stating he is a capitalist. "I'm not a socialist. I'm just a capitalist who understands how capitalism works," he said.

El-Sayed emphasized his views on capitalism as a point of difference from self-described democratic socialist Bernie Sanders. 

In a recent interview with The New York Times, he responded to Trump's claims that he is a communist by saying: "The man is so clearly a joker."

In a comment to DW, Lawrence Pintak also called the claims historically bizarre. He sees it as part of systematic attempts by the Republican Party "to spin 'progressive' and 'democratic socialist' to be synonyms for 'Communist.'"

An analysis by Reuters found that Trump has significantly increased his use of the term in recent weeks.

Pintak told DW that the loaded term works well on social media.

Misattributing views on 9/11

Claim: After El-Sayed secured the Democratic nomination, his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, posted a statement on X, calling him "someone who believes America deserved 9/11."

DW Fact check: False

9/11 refers to the terrorist attacks on September 11, 2001, in which planes hijacked by militant ​al-Qaeda Islamists struck the World Trade Center in New York and the Pentagon near Washington, killing nearly 3,000 people.

The allegation has come up repeatedly but conflates previous remarks made by El-Sayed supporter Hasan Piker with El-Sayed's own views.

Piker has supported El-Sayed during his 2026 US Senate campaign, appearing with him at rallies and in livestreams.

During a 2019 livestream, Piker said America had "deserved" 9/11, a remark that generated widespread criticism. Since then, however, he has walked back this statement.

When asked by US-based fact checkers PolitiFactfor evidence to support his claim, the Rogers campaign pointed to a video clip of El-Sayed refusing to disavow Piker's 2019 comments. 

Pintak, who researches Islamophobia, described "guilt by association" as one of the disinformation tactics used against El-Sayed.

He points out that El-Sayed has become a target of disinformation at a time when the Republican Party has shifted from an anti-immigrant focus back to an anti-Muslim narrative. 

"Attacks on Muslim candidates, and El-Sayed himself, are nothing new," Pintak said, pointing to Islamophobic reporting during El-Sayed's 2018 campaign for Michigan governor and false claims portraying New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani as an extremist.

During the 2018 midterms, Pintak led a research team that found Muslim candidates, from local school boards to Congress, were systematically targeted by "a social media narrative of manufactured outrage [that] was disproportionately Islamophobic, xenophobic, racist, and misogynistic." 

The researchers concluded that such attacks were often aimed at undermining candidates' legitimacy and reducing trust among voters.

entries.title: Can a giant Madonna help slow secularization in Poland?
entries.summary: Europe's largest statue of the Virgin Mary will be inaugurated on Saturday in the Polish village of Konotopie. What will the monument mean for the village it towers over and for the Catholic faith in Poland in general?
entries.content:
Poland

Can a giant Madonna help slow secularization in Poland?

August 14, 2026

Europe's largest statue of the Virgin Mary will be inaugurated on Saturday in the Polish village of Konotopie. What will the monument mean for the village it towers over and for the Catholic faith in Poland in general?

With its grain fields, meadows and lake, the countryside around the tiny village of Konotopie in central Poland is idyllic. Now there is a monumental statue of the Virgin Mary towering above all this.

Home to just 120 residents and situated about 160 kilometers (99 miles) northwest of the capital, Warsaw, the previously little-known village of Konotopie has been in the headlines for weeks now as a result of the massive statue.

The snow-white structure, which is visible for miles around, is more than 55 meters (180 feet) tall. The statue itself is 40.6 meters high and stands on a 15-meter-high pedestal shaped like a crown that is intended to serve as a viewing platform.

The figure dwarfs Rio de Janeiro's famous statue of Christ the Redeemer, which reaches a total height of 38 meters including its base.

'Pile of concrete' or 'fantastic achievement?'

The statue will be officially inaugurated on Saturday, August 15, the feast of the Assumption of Mary, a major holy day in the Catholic calendar.

Although final construction work is still underway and the site remains fenced off and guarded, thousands of people — both pilgrims and sightseers — have been flocking to see it for months.

Opinion about the project is divided.

"It's a nightmare," one critic of the statue told the weekly magazine Newsweek, "a complete waste. Instead of investing that money in useful projects, they financed a giant pile of concrete."

"This Mary is absolutely beautiful. My utmost respect. A fantastic achievement," said one devout woman visiting the site, according to the right-wing conservative weekly Sieci.

Madonna statue financed by Poland's Warren Buffett

The benefactor behind the statue, 75-year-old Roman Karkosik, hails from a nearby village and is one of Poland's wealthiest individuals.

Nearly 40 years ago, when the shortage economy of socialism gave way to free-market capitalism after the collapse of communism in eastern Europe, Karkosik was a young graduate from technical high school.

He started out as a bartender, but moved on to buying and selling scrap metal, producing soft drinks and later became the first entrepreneur in Poland to manufacture plastic bottles.

Karkosik made a name for himself on the Warsaw Stock Exchange. Some journalists have compared his role in Poland to Warren Buffett's influence on Wall Street.

His fortune is estimated at roughly €442 million ($511 million), and he ranks 44th on Wprost magazine's list of Poland's richest people. He lives in an 18th-century manor in the town of Kikol, just two kilometers from Konotopie.

A 'gesture of gratitude'

Karkosik and his wife, Grazyna, avoid both public appearances and contact with the media.

The cost of the statue remains a closely guarded secret. Media reports speculate that the project may have cost as much as €23 million.

The Karkosiks have described the Marian statue as a "gesture of gratitude."

According to media reports, the devout businessman wanted to thank the Virgin Mary for his recovery from a serious illness. His two brothers, who were also successful businessmen, both died prematurely after illnesses.

This is not the first time Karkosik has provided money for a religious structure. Back in 2011, he funded the construction of a church at a nearby pilgrimage site.

Artist feared seeing the finished statue

"I was afraid to come to Konotopie to see what had become of my design in reality," sculptor Adam Jakub Matejkowski told Polish media. Worried that the hands and face of the Virgin Mary might appear distorted, Matejkowski only visited the site in July.

"I opened my eyes and was stunned. The Mother of God is opening her arms to embrace us," he said with satisfaction. "That was exactly my intention: for the figure to have a human character, to come toward us."

Matejkowski says the statue has the facial expression of his 11-year-old daughter and the delicate facial features of his wife.

Polish region hopes for economic boost

Konotopie is situated in one of Poland's economically weak regions. There are no major industrial employers here, and jobs are scarce.

Local leaders hope the Marian statue will stimulate economic growth.

"The monument is not only a spiritual landmark but also a strategic asset for the region. We expect it to attract more investors and tourists, which will benefit the local economy," Krzysztof Kowalewski of the authorities in the nearby town of Kikol told Polish media.

Mayor Renata Golebiewska has said that revenues at local restaurants and bars have already broken local records.

Not the first statue of its kind in Poland

Poland is well known for its monumental Christian structures.

Following Poland's transition to democracy in 1989, a massive basilica was built in the village of Lichen in central Poland, overshadowing even the cathedrals of Paris and Cologne in scale.

The basilica is 138 meters (453 feet) long, 77 meters wide, and features a dome with a diameter of 35 meters. It can accommodate 20,000 worshippers.

Since 2010, Poland has also been home to the world's tallest statue of Jesus. Located in Swiebodzin near the German border, the 36-meter-high statue stands on a 17-meter-high mound.

Rising secularization

Whether all these gigantic monuments can stop the ongoing secularization of Polish society, however, remains highly questionable.

Although Poland is still one of the most Catholic countries in Europe, public trust in the Church continues to decline.

For centuries, the Catholic faith was a key part of Polish identity.

In the 19th century, when the territory that now makes up Poland was not an independent state and was divided up among foreign powers, Catholicism played a major role in the resistance to Protestant Prussia and Orthodox Russia.

After World War II, despite ideological differences, the anti-communist opposition and the Catholic Church in Poland worked together against the communist dictatorship.

During this period, churches became refuges for persecuted dissidents, and several priests were murdered by the secret police.

Pope John Paul II, himself Polish, also played a significant role in the struggle against the regime.

Catholicism in modern-day Poland

Since Poland's transition to democracy in 1989, however, the Catholic Church has experienced a crisis similar to that seen across Europe.

According to a September 2025 survey conducted by the Polish polling institute IBRIS, only 35% of Poles still trust the Church, down from 58% in 2016. Distrust rose from 24% to 47% over the same period.

In 2026, the annual number of priests ordained in Poland fell below 200 for the first time since 2000. Church attendance has also been steadily declining, especially among young people.

Even a gigantic Madonna is unlikely to reverse that trend.

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: NATO jets shoot down drone over Latvia
entries.summary: Jets have shot down a foreign drone over Latvia after it entered the Baltic state's airspace. Its origin remains unclear, but the incident adds to concern over repeated incursions along NATO's eastern flank.
entries.content:
Latvia

NATO jets shoot down drone over Latvia

August 14, 2026

Jets have shot down a foreign drone over Latvia after it entered the Baltic state's airspace. Its origin remains unclear, but the incident adds to concern over repeated incursions along NATO's eastern flank.

NATO fighter jets have shot down a drone that entered Latvian airspace, the alliance and Latvian authorities said Friday.

Two Italian Eurofighters were scrambled and one destroyed the unmanned aircraft, while two Turkish F-16s were also deployed under NATO command.

What happened over Latvia?

Latvia's military initially issued an air alert and urged people in affected areas to remain indoors and seek shelter.

Authorities said the foreign drone entered Latvian airspace over the Balvi region as a result of Russian electronic warfare activity.

It was not immediately clear where the drone originated, and NATO said an investigation was underway.

Latvian authorities did not identify the drone as Ukrainian.

However, the reference to Russian electronic warfare raised the possibility that a Ukrainian drone targeting Russia had been forced off course by interference.

Ukrainian forces had attacked targets in northwestern Russia overnight, according to Latvian media.

Has this happened before?

Latvia and other NATO countries along the alliance's eastern flank have faced repeated incursions by drones since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

A stray drone was also shot down over Latvia in early June, while other Ukrainian drones heading toward northwestern Russia have previously entered Latvian airspace and crashed.

Romanian and Spanish fighter jets were also deployed on Thursday after drones entered Romanian airspace near Ukraine.

Why are Italian jets defending Latvian airspace?

Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania do not operate their own fighter aircraft, so NATO allies rotate responsibility for policing their skies.

The Italian Eurofighters involved in Friday's interception are based at Siauliai air base in Lithuania.

If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.
